text: Sweet Briar College, located in Sweet Briar, Amherst County, Virginia, is a private women's liberal arts college established in 1901 by Indiana Fletcher Williams in memory of her daughter, Daisy. The college formally opened in 1906 and granted its first Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree in 1910. It nearly closed on August 25, 2015, due to insurmountable financial challenges, including declining enrollment and an endowment that dropped from $96.2 million in 2011 to $84 million by March 2015, with only $19 million unrestricted, $18 million temporarily restricted, and $53 million permanently restricted. The college faced about $25 million in debt and was at risk of default. The board cited a declining interest in the traditional women's college model and explored merging with institutions like the University of Virginia, but no merger occurred. A group of alumnae, students, faculty, and supporters launched "Saving Sweet Briar" to prevent closure through legal action, social media, and fundraising, arguing the financial decline was overstated. Legal challenges followed, including lawsuits from faculty seeking $42 million in damages and reinstatement, and a separate lawsuit by the Amherst County Attorney on behalf of the Commonwealth of Virginia, which initially failed to halt the closure but was later supported by the Virginia Supreme Court, leading to a temporary injunction. A mediation agreement in June 2015 resulted in the resignation of President James F. Jones and at least 13 board members, with Saving Sweet Briar appointing a new board and Phillip Stone as president. Stone, who stated he did not regard the appointment as interim, aimed to increase enrollment beyond past highs and invited most faculty and staff to remain, offering six months' severance for those who left. Saving Sweet Briar contributed $12 million by September 2015, and the state Attorney General released $16 million in endowment funds, though the college later decided not to draw on it. Stone stepped down in April 2016, and Meredith Jung-En Woo became president in May 2017. Under Woo, the college restructured its curriculum in fall 2018 by eliminating historic departments and replacing them with three centers: Engineering, Science and Technology in Society; Human and Environmental Sustainability; and Creativity, Design and the Arts, replacing traditional general education with a core curriculum centered on women's leadership. Semesters were changed to a 3-12-12-3 format to allow focus on intensive classes, study abroad, and research. In January 2016, the college received over 1,000 applications for the 2016–2017 academic year and maintained its commitment not to use the $16 million in restricted funds. In June 2018, the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges placed Sweet Briar on "warning" status due to fiscal-year 2017 finances, requiring a demonstration of sound financial management within 12 months, which was lifted in June 2019. In August 2024, the college announced it would not accept transgender students, requiring applicants to confirm their sex assigned at birth is female and that they live and identify as a woman, a policy criticized by student groups and the faculty senate, which approved a resolution supporting transgender student inclusion and described the policy as "morally repugnant." The college offers 17 majors, 21 minors, 3 preprofessional programs (pre-law, pre-medicine, pre-veterinary), 2 certificate programs (arts management, equine studies), teacher licensure in 10 areas, and one graduate degree (Master of Arts in Teaching). It offers B.A., B.F.A., and B.S. degrees and is the second women's college to offer an ABET-accredited engineering degree. With a student/faculty ratio of 9 to 1 and 84% of classes having fewer than 20 students, Sweet Briar was tied for #29 in Most Innovative Schools and #35 in Top Performers on Social Mobility in 2023 according to U.S. News & World Report. The college provides several study abroad programs, including the Junior Year in France (JYF), Japanese Studies at Doshisha, a program in China-Beijing, the Intercollegiate Center of Classical Studies in Rome, the American School of Classical Studies in Athens, the National Security Education Program in multiple countries, and others, with credit available for international internships. It also offers academic fellowships and grants to students.

Sweet Briar College offers an accredited engineering degree. The student/faculty ratio is 9 to 1, with 84% of classes having fewer than 20 students. In 2023, U.S. News & World Report ranked Sweet Briar tied for #29 in Most Innovative Schools and tied for #35 in Top Performers on Social Mobility, both out of 210 national liberal arts colleges. The college provides several study abroad programs, including the Junior Year in France (JYF), the Japanese Studies Program at Doshisha Women's College of Liberal Arts, the Wake Forest/Southern Atlantic States Association for Asian and African Studies (SASASAAS) Program in China-Beijing, the Intercollegiate Center of Classical Studies in Rome, the American School of Classical Studies Summer Program at Athens, the National Security Education Program (NSEP) in multiple countries, and other international programs; students can earn credit for international internships with approval. Sweet Briar offers academic fellowships and grants for its students. In 2024, the college accepted 75.7% of undergraduate applicants, with admission standards considered difficult and enrolled students having an average 3.54 high school GPA; standardized test scores are not required, though those who submitted had an average SAT score of 1190 (22% submitting) or average ACT score of 26 (15% submitting). U.S. News & World Report ranks Sweet Briar tied for No. 173 out of 211 National Liberal Arts Colleges, tied for No. 56 in Best Undergraduate Teaching, and tied for No. 78 in Top Performers on Social Mobility. The college's architecture is primarily the work of Ralph Adams Cram, who also designed campuses at Princeton University and West Point; although known for Gothic Revival, Cram designed Sweet Briar in the Colonial Revival style using red brick buildings with white balustrades and arcades. Twenty-one of the thirty campus buildings are part of the "Sweet Briar College Historic District" designated by the National Register of Historic Places, including Sweet Briar House, which houses the college president. The campus includes the Sweet Briar plantation burial ground (slave cemetery), where upwards of 60 slaves are buried; archaeologists have uncovered many slave artifacts, and a slave cabin from the 1840s, also used by early college employees, is located behind Sweet Briar House. Many faculty and staff live on campus in homes they rent or privately own, on land owned by the college. Sweet Briar is a residential campus with nearly all students living on campus; there are seven standard dormitories and additional independent living options for upperclasswomen in the Green Village and Patterson House. The college has over 50 clubs and organizations. Like other women's colleges, Sweet Briar has traditions, most notably Founder's Day, when students, faculty, and staff walk to Monument Hill to place daisies at Daisy Williams's grave site and memorial. The athletic teams are known as the Vixens, and the college competes in Division III of the NCAA, primarily in the Old Dominion Athletic Conference (ODAC) since the 1982–83 academic year. Sweet Briar competes in nine intercollegiate varsity sports: women's sports include cross country, equestrian, field hockey, golf, lacrosse, soccer, softball, swimming, and tennis; fencing is a club sport. Students also participate in recreational sports through the Sweet Briar Outdoor Program (SWEBOP), which organizes trips for hiking, fly fishing, caving, rock climbing, and weekly kayaking and skiing. The college is known for its horseback riding program, which focuses on show and field hunters, hunt seat equitation, and show jumping; it has seven riding teams, including a jumper team, a hunter show team, a JV hunter show team, an American National Riding Commission (ANRC) team, a field team, and an Intercollegiate Horse Show Association (IHSA) team. Students can study for an Equine Studies Certificate with a focus in training or equine management. Sweet Briar hosted the 23rd Annual ANRC Intercollegiate Equitation Championship in 2000, judged by Victor Hugo Vidal & Dacia Funkhouser, and the 37th Annual ANRC Intercollegiate Equitation Championship in 2014, judged by George H. Morris. The college has earned four ODAC titles (1987, 2012, 2015, 2016), nine ANRC team national championship titles (1978–1980; 1986–1990; 1999), and 10 ANRC team reserve national championship titles (1981–1985; 2000–2002; 2004–2005); students have been individual national champions nine times and individual reserve ANRC national champions seven times. In 2006, Sweet Briar's IHSA team won their region (Zone 4, Region 1), placed second at Zones, qualifying for Nationals, where they placed third overall. In 2008, the IHSA team won their region and advanced to Nationals, where team members earned individual ribbons.
